claim: MITF is the master regulator of the melanocyte lineage.
source: Microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF) is the master regulator of the melanocyte lineage.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about MITF's role.

claim: MITF interacts with a PBAF chromatin remodelling complex comprising BRG1 and CHD7.
source: We show that MITF interacts with a PBAF chromatin remodelling complex comprising BRG1 and CHD7.
evidence: This claim is supported by tandem affinity purification and mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript, as well as co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: BRG1 is essential for melanoma cell proliferation in vitro.
source: BRG1 is essential for melanoma cell proliferation in vitro and for normal melanocyte development in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that BRG1 knockdown arrests 501Mel proliferation and induces senescence, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: BRG1 is essential for normal melanocyte development in vivo.
source: BRG1 is essential for melanoma cell proliferation in vitro and for normal melanocyte development in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by mouse genetic experiments showing that Tyr-Cre::Smarca4mel−/− mice lack pigmentation and identifiable melanocytes, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: MITF and SOX10 actively recruit BRG1 to MITF-associated regulatory elements (MAREs) at active enhancers.
source: MITF and SOX10 actively recruit BRG1 to a set of MITF-associated regulatory elements (MAREs) at active enhancers.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing loss of BRG1 occupancy upon siRNA-mediated silencing of MITF or SOX10, as shown in Figure 8.

claim: Combinations of MITF, SOX10, TFAP2A, and YY1 bind between two BRG1-occupied nucleosomes.
source: Combinations of MITF, SOX10, TFAP2A, and YY1 bind between two BRG1-occupied nucleosomes thus defining both a signature of transcription factors essential for the melanocyte lineage and a specific chromatin organisation of the regulatory elements they occupy.
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis showing co-localization patterns of these factors with BRG1, as shown in Figures 7 and 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: BRG1 regulates the dynamics of MITF genomic occupancy.
source: BRG1 also regulates the dynamics of MITF genomic occupancy.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing increased MITF occupancy at co-occupied sites following BRG1 silencing, as shown in Figure 9.

claim: MITF regulates specification, survival, and proliferation of normal melanocytes.
source: Microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF), a basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLH-Zip) factor, regulates specification, survival, and proliferation of normal melanocytes, and controls proliferation, migration and invasion of melanoma cells (Goding, 2000; Widlund and Fisher, 2003; Steingrimsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MITF controls proliferation, migration and invasion of melanoma cells.
source: Microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF), a basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLH-Zip) factor, regulates specification, survival, and proliferation of normal melanocytes, and controls proliferation, migration and invasion of melanoma cells (Goding, 2000; Widlund and Fisher, 2003; Steingrimsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: siRNA-mediated MITF silencing induces senescence in several melanoma lines.
source: siRNA-mediated MITF silencing induces senescence in several melanoma lines (Strub et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: MITF directly and positively regulates genes involved in DNA replication and repair and mitosis.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation coupled to deep sequencing (ChIP-seq) identified MITF binding sites and integration with RNA-seq following siRNA-mediated MITF knockdown showed that MITF directly and positively regulates genes involved in DNA replication and repair and mitosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous ChIP-seq and RNA-seq work by the authors.

claim: MITF represses genes involved in melanoma invasion.
source: In contrast, MITF represses genes involved in melanoma invasion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: MITF heterodimerizes with TFEB, TFE3 and TFEC.
source: Previously described MITF partners such as its heterodimerisation partners TFEB, TFE3 and TFEC (Steingrimsson et al., 2002) and its cofactor β-catenin (CTNNB1) (Schepsky et al., 2006) (Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1) were detected.
evidence: This is supported by both citation to previous literature and detection in the current mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: β-catenin (CTNNB1) is a cofactor of MITF.
source: Previously described MITF partners such as its heterodimerisation partners TFEB, TFE3 and TFEC (Steingrimsson et al., 2002) and its cofactor β-catenin (CTNNB1) (Schepsky et al., 2006) (Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1) were detected.
evidence: This is supported by both citation to previous literature and detection in the current mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: MITF interacts with components of the NURF chromatin-remodelling complex including BPTF, SMARCA1 (SNF2L), SMARCA5 (SNF2H), and RBBP4.
source: The BPTF, SMARCA1 (SNF2L), SMARCA5 (SNF2H), and RBBP4 components of the NURF chromatin-remodelling complex associated with MITF specifically in the chromatin fraction.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from tandem affinity purification experiments.

claim: MITF interacts with DNA damage response machinery including XRCC5, XRCC6, PRKDC, BRCA2, MSH2 and MSH6.
source: Components of the DNA damage response machinery including XRCC5 and XRCC6 (Ku80 and Ku70), DNA-dependent protein kinase (PRKDC), BRCA2 as well as MSH2 and MSH6 were identified along with the HECT domain-containing E3-ligase HERC2, previously implicated in DNA repair (Bekker-Jensen et al., 2010), and UBR5 a second HECT domain-containing E3-ligase with functions in both DNA repair and transcription (Cojocaru et al., 2011; Gudjonsson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from tandem affinity purification experiments.

claim: MITF interacts with HERC2, an E3-ligase previously implicated in DNA repair.
source: Components of the DNA damage response machinery including XRCC5 and XRCC6 (Ku80 and Ku70), DNA-dependent protein kinase (PRKDC), BRCA2 as well as MSH2 and MSH6 were identified along with the HECT domain-containing E3-ligase HERC2, previously implicated in DNA repair (Bekker-Jensen et al., 2010), and UBR5 a second HECT domain-containing E3-ligase with functions in both DNA repair and transcription (Cojocaru et al., 2011; Gudjonsson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry and immunoblot data.

claim: MITF interacts with de-ubiquitinase enzymes USP7 and USP11.
source: NEURL4, a known HERC2-interacting protein (Al-Hakim et al., 2012), was also found along with the de-ubiquitinase enzymes USP7 and USP11 that were preferentially represented in the SNE.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry and immunoblot data showing their presence in MITF immunoprecipitations.

claim: USP13 was not detected in MITF immunoprecipitations.
source: In contrast, USP13 shown to regulate MITF stability (Zhao et al., 2011) was not detected in our experiments.
evidence: This is based on the absence of detection in mass spectrometry experiments, contrasting with previous literature showing USP13 regulates MITF stability.

claim: MITF interacts with four subunits of TFIIIC, a RNA polymerase III cofactor.
source: We identified several other complexes interacting with MITF. Four subunits of TFIIIC, a RNA polymerase III cofactor were detected along with the SMCA1, SMC3, STAG2, and PDS5 cohesin subunits.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from tandem affinity purification experiments.

claim: MITF interacts with cohesin subunits SMCA1, SMC3, STAG2, and PDS5.
source: We identified several other complexes interacting with MITF. Four subunits of TFIIIC, a RNA polymerase III cofactor were detected along with the SMCA1, SMC3, STAG2, and PDS5 cohesin subunits.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from tandem affinity purification experiments.

claim: MITF interacts with TRIM28 (TIF1β, KAP1), a co-repressor.
source: TRIM28 (TIF1β, KAP1), a co-repressor belonging to a sub-family of TRIM proteins comprising TRIM24 (TIF1α) and TRIM33 (TIF1γ) was found as were the HDAC1 and HDAC2 and the HP1 proteins known to associate with TRIM-co-repressor complexes (Herquel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from tandem affinity purification experiments.

claim: MITF interacts with HDAC1 and HDAC2.
source: TRIM28 (TIF1β, KAP1), a co-repressor belonging to a sub-family of TRIM proteins comprising TRIM24 (TIF1α) and TRIM33 (TIF1γ) was found as were the HDAC1 and HDAC2 and the HP1 proteins known to associate with TRIM-co-repressor complexes (Herquel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from tandem affinity purification experiments.

claim: MITF interacts with TRRAP, RUVBL1, RUVBL2, and BAF53A.
source: We identified TRRAP, RUVBL1, RUVBL2, and BAF53A. These proteins are already known to form a cofactor for MYC (Park et al., 2001, 2002; Murr et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from tandem affinity purification experiments.

claim: A mutation in TRRAP has been associated with human melanoma.
source: Interestingly, a mutation in TRRAP has recently been associated with human melanoma (Wei et al., 2011) that together with its interaction with MITF suggests a role in melanomagenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: MITF interacts with DNA replication factor C subunits RFC1, RFC2, RFC4, and RFC5.
source: In addition to transcription complexes, the RFC1, RFC2, RFC4, and RFC5 subunits of DNA replication factor C associate with MITF along with the MCM3, MCM5, and MCM7 subunits of the MCM complex that forms at DNA-replication origins.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from tandem affinity purification experiments.

claim: MITF interacts with MCM complex subunits MCM3, MCM5, and MCM7.
source: In addition to transcription complexes, the RFC1, RFC2, RFC4, and RFC5 subunits of DNA replication factor C associate with MITF along with the MCM3, MCM5, and MCM7 subunits of the MCM complex that forms at DNA-replication origins.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from tandem affinity purification experiments.

claim: MITF interacts with AKAP8 and AKAP8L.
source: AKAP8 and AKAP8L were also identified and AKAP8 has been shown to interact with the MCM complex (Eide et al., 2003), although these protein kinase A anchoring proteins have additional functions (Collas et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from tandem affinity purification experiments.

claim: MITF interacts with the kinase PLK1 in the chromatin-associated fraction.
source: The kinase PLK1 was found in the chromatin-associated fraction suggesting that it may phosphorylate MITF on chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from tandem affinity purification experiments.

claim: MITF interacts with multiple subunits of the nuclear pore complex.
source: Finally, we detected multiple subunits of the nuclear pore complex. This may reflect control of MITF sub-cellular localization or a coupling of MITF-driven transcription and RNA-export.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data, though the functional significance is speculative.

claim: BRG1 was reported to interact with MITF.
source: While BRG1 was reported to interact with MITF (de la Serna et al., 2006; Keenen et al., 2010), the composition of the complex had not been determined.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The MITF-interacting complex comprises BRG1, PBRM1 (BAF180), SMARCC2 (BAF170), SMARCD2 (BAF60B), and ACTL6A (BAF53A).
source: We identified BRG1 (SMARCA4) as well as the PBRM1 (BAF180), SMARCC2 (BAF170), SMARCD2 (BAF60B), and ACTL6A (BAF53A) subunits along with CHD7 reported to associate with BRG1 in human neural crest cells (Bajpai et al., 2010) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from tandem affinity purification experiments.

claim: CHD7 associates with BRG1 in human neural crest cells.
source: We identified BRG1 (SMARCA4) as well as the PBRM1 (BAF180), SMARCC2 (BAF170), SMARCD2 (BAF60B), and ACTL6A (BAF53A) subunits along with CHD7 reported to associate with BRG1 in human neural crest cells (Bajpai et al., 2010) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The MITF interacting complex most closely resembles the PBAF variant with the presence of PBRM1.
source: The MITF interacting complex most closely resembles the PBAF variant with the presence of PBRM1 (Trotter and Archer, 2008; Reisman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on the identification of PBRM1 in the complex and comparison with known complex compositions from the literature.

claim: BRG1 co-precipitates with BAF200, BAF155, BAF53A, BAF180, and BAF170 in 501Mel cells.
source: To investigate BRG1 complex composition in 501Mel cells, extracts were precipitated with an anti-BRG1 antibody showing co-precipitation of BRG1 with BAF200, BAF155, BAF53A, BAF180, and BAF170, whereas BAF60B and BAF250B were not co-precipitated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: BAF60B and BAF250B do not co-precipitate with BRG1 in 501Mel cells.
source: To investigate BRG1 complex composition in 501Mel cells, extracts were precipitated with an anti-BRG1 antibody showing co-precipitation of BRG1 with BAF200, BAF155, BAF53A, BAF180, and BAF170, whereas BAF60B and BAF250B were not co-precipitated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: BRG1 and CHD7 reciprocally co-precipitate with each other.
source: The MITF-interacting complex also comprises CHD7 as seen by the reciprocal co-precipitation of BRG1 and CHD7 and their co-precipitation with MITF (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: BRG1 and CHD7 co-precipitate with MITF.
source: The MITF-interacting complex also comprises CHD7 as seen by the reciprocal co-precipitation of BRG1 and CHD7 and their co-precipitation with MITF (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: BRG1 knockdown strongly reduces MITF protein and mRNA levels.
source: si/shRNA knockdown of BRG1 strongly reduced MITF protein and mRNA levels (Vachtenheim et al., 2010 and Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and RT-qPCR data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: BRG1 silencing reduces expression of MITF target genes involved in cell cycle, pigmentation and signalling.
source: The effects of BRG1 silencing on gene expression were therefore very similar to the loss of MITF itself with reduced expression of MITF target genes involved in cell cycle, pigmentation and signalling and activation of several genes of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) whose expression is also induced upon MITF-knockdown (Ohanna et al., 2011) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: BRG1 silencing activates genes of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).
source: The effects of BRG1 silencing on gene expression were therefore very similar to the loss of MITF itself with reduced expression of MITF target genes involved in cell cycle, pigmentation and signalling and activation of several genes of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) whose expression is also induced upon MITF-knockdown (Ohanna et al., 2011) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B and citation to previous work.

claim: BRG1 silencing arrests 501Mel proliferation.
source: BRG1 silencing arrested 501Mel proliferation and cells showed a flattened enlarged morphology with multiple cytoplasmic projections, similar to senescent cells upon MITF knockdown (Figure 3C [Strub et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 3C.

claim: BRG1 knockdown cells show a flattened enlarged morphology with multiple cytoplasmic projections.
source: BRG1 silencing arrested 501Mel proliferation and cells showed a flattened enlarged morphology with multiple cytoplasmic projections, similar to senescent cells upon MITF knockdown (Figure 3C [Strub et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Up to 40% of BRG1 knockdown cells show senescence-associated β-galactosidase staining.
source: Up to 40% of the BRG1 knockdown cells showed senescence-associated β-galactosidase staining (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ShBRG1 silencing down-regulates more than 4000 genes in 501Mel cells.
source: RNA-seq following shBRG1 silencing revealed a dramatic effect on gene expression with >4000 genes down-regulated and >5400 genes up-regulated (p.adj <0.05 and log2fold change >1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: ShBRG1 silencing up-regulates more than 5400 genes in 501Mel cells.
source: RNA-seq following shBRG1 silencing revealed a dramatic effect on gene expression with >4000 genes down-regulated and >5400 genes up-regulated (p.adj <0.05 and log2fold change >1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: ShMITF knockdown down-regulates around 600 genes in 501Mel cells.
source: ShMITF knockdown resulted in cell cycle arrest and morphological changes associated with senescence (Figure 3C) accompanied by the down-regulation of around 600 genes and up-regulation of 747 genes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: ShMITF knockdown up-regulates 747 genes in 501Mel cells.
source: ShMITF knockdown resulted in cell cycle arrest and morphological changes associated with senescence (Figure 3C) accompanied by the down-regulation of around 600 genes and up-regulation of 747 genes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: 60% of genes down-regulated by shMITF show similar loss of expression upon shBRG1.
source: 60% of genes down-regulated by shMITF showed similar loss of expression upon shBRG1 consistent with the fact that MITF was strongly repressed in the shBRG1 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by comparative RNA-seq analysis.

claim: SOX10 expression is strongly repressed in BRG1 knockdown cells.
source: We noted that SOX10 expression is strongly repressed in BRG1 knockdown cells, but not in MITF-knockdown cells (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: SOX10 expression is not repressed in MITF-knockdown cells.
source: We noted that SOX10 expression is strongly repressed in BRG1 knockdown cells, but not in MITF-knockdown cells (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: SiSOX10 silencing represses endogenous MITF expression.
source: SiSOX10 silencing repressed endogenous MITF expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: In 501Mel-Cl8 cells, siSOX10 represses endogenous MITF but not ectopic MITF.
source: In 501Mel-Cl8 cells constitutively expressing 3HA-tagged MITF from the CMV promoter (Strub et al., 2011), siSOX10 repressed endogenous, but not ectopic MITF.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in 501Mel-Cl8 cells expressing ectopic MITF.

claim: SiCREB silencing has no effect on MITF expression.
source: In contrast, siCREB silencing had no effect on MITF expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: SOX10 is a major regulator of MITF expression in 501Mel cells.
source: SOX10 is therefore a major regulator of MITF expression in 501Mel cells and its diminished expression upon BRG1 knockdown partly explains the concomitant MITF loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing SOX10 knockdown represses MITF and that BRG1 knockdown represses SOX10.

claim: SOX10 promotes melanoma cell proliferation.
source: These observations are also consistent with previous reports showing that SOX10 promotes melanoma cell proliferation and that its loss leads to senescence (Cronin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Loss of SOX10 leads to senescence.
source: These observations are also consistent with previous reports showing that SOX10 promotes melanoma cell proliferation and that its loss leads to senescence (Cronin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: BRG1 acts as an MITF co-factor.
source: To determine whether the shared phenotypes of BRG1 and MITF knockdown cells resulted from the concomitant loss of MITF upon BRG1 silencing or whether BRG1 acts also as an MITF co-factor, we performed shBRG1 silencing in the 501Mel-Cl8 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing that BRG1 knockdown in cells with ectopic MITF still results in loss of MITF target gene expression.

claim: BRG1 knockdown in 501Mel-Cl8 cells represses endogenous MITF but not ectopic 3HA-MITF.
source: BRG1 knockdown in these cells repressed endogenous MITF expression, but not ectopic 3HA-MITF (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: BRG1 silencing elicits arrested proliferation and morphological changes in 501Mel-Cl8 cells.
source: Nevertheless, BRG1 silencing elicited a phenotype similar to 501Mel cells characterised by arrested proliferation, and morphological changes.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations.

claim: Many MITF target genes are repressed by BRG1 silencing in both 501Mel and Cl8 cells.
source: Many MITF target genes were similarly repressed by BRG1 silencing in both 501Mel and Cl8 cells, while SASP components were induced (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Ectopic MITF in Cl8 cells does not activate target genes in the absence of BRG1.
source: Together, these data show that BRG1 is essential for MITF expression and that it acts as a cofactor for MITF since ectopic MITF in the Cl8 cells does not activate target genes expression in its absence.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that ectopic MITF cannot rescue target gene expression when BRG1 is knocked down.

claim: ShBRG1 silencing has little effect on MITF expression in Hermes 3A cells.
source: In contrast to 501Mel cells, shBRG1 silencing had little effect on MITF expression in Hermes 3A cells (Figure 3D), but induced changes in cell morphology with up to 80% of cells showing staining for senescence-associated β-galactosidase (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ShBRG1 silencing induces changes in cell morphology in Hermes 3A cells with up to 80% showing senescence-associated β-galactosidase staining.
source: In contrast to 501Mel cells, shBRG1 silencing had little effect on MITF expression in Hermes 3A cells (Figure 3D), but induced changes in cell morphology with up to 80% of cells showing staining for senescence-associated β-galactosidase (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: BRG1-silenced Hermes 3A cells detach from the plate within 8 days.
source: Within 8 days, the BRG1 silenced cells detached from the plate.
evidence: This is based on observation of cell culture.

claim: ShMITF silencing in Hermes 3A cells leads to growth arrest and marked changes in morphology.
source: ShMITF silencing in Hermes 3A cells also led to growth arrest and a marked changes in morphology, with flattening, enlargement of the cell body and reduced neurite projections (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Less than 50% of shMITF-silenced Hermes 3A cells show senescence-associated β-galactosidase staining.
source: Despite these changes indicative of senescence, <50% of shMITF-silenced cells showed staining for senescence-associated β-galactosidase.
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase staining data.

claim: MITF-silenced Hermes 3A cells detach from the plate within 7 days.
source: As with shBRG1, MITF silencing led to cells detaching from the plate within 7 days.
evidence: This is based on observation of cell culture.

claim: Both BRG1 and MITF are essential for melanocyte growth.
source: Thus, both BRG1 and MITF are essential for melanocyte growth, and in their absence cells undergo growth arrest, senescence, and death.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that knockdown of either factor leads to growth arrest, senescence, and cell death.

claim: BRG1 silencing in Hermes 3A cells down-regulates 587 genes.
source: RNA-seq showed that BRG1 silencing in Hermes 3A cells down-regulated 587 genes, and up-regulated 971 genes, many fewer than in 501Mel cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: BRG1 silencing in Hermes 3A cells up-regulates 971 genes.
source: RNA-seq showed that BRG1 silencing in Hermes 3A cells down-regulated 587 genes, and up-regulated 971 genes, many fewer than in 501Mel cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: MITF silencing in Hermes 3A cells down-regulates 757 genes.
source: MITF silencing down-regulated 757 genes and up-regulated 664 genes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: MITF silencing in Hermes 3A cells up-regulates 664 genes.
source: MITF silencing down-regulated 757 genes and up-regulated 664 genes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: 38% of genes down-regulated upon BRG1 silencing in Hermes 3A cells are diminished by MITF silencing.
source: Comparisons showed that 38% of genes down-regulated upon BRG1 silencing were diminished by MITF silencing, while 25% of the BRG1 up-regulated genes were also increased upon MITF silencing.
evidence: This is supported by comparative RNA-seq analysis.

claim: 25% of BRG1 up-regulated genes in Hermes 3A cells are also increased upon MITF silencing.
source: Comparisons showed that 38% of genes down-regulated upon BRG1 silencing were diminished by MITF silencing, while 25% of the BRG1 up-regulated genes were also increased upon MITF silencing.
evidence: This is supported by comparative RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Tyr-Cre::Smarca4mel−/− mice are present in the progeny at the expected ratio.
source: The Tyr-Cre::Smarca4mel−/− mice were present in the progeny at the expected ratio indicating no loss of viability (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Heterozygous Tyr-Cre::Smarca4mel+/− mice are black.
source: While the heterozygous Tyr-Cre::Smarca4mel+/− mice were black, homozygous Tyr-Cre::Smarca4mel−/− mice were either completely white or had occasional black spotting presumably arising from rare melanoblasts that had escaped Cre-driven recombination during embryogenesis (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by photographs of mice shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Homozygous Tyr-Cre::Smarca4mel−/− mice are either completely white or have occasional black spotting.
source: While the heterozygous Tyr-Cre::Smarca4mel+/− mice were black, homozygous Tyr-Cre::Smarca4mel−/− mice were either completely white or had occasional black spotting presumably arising from rare melanoblasts that had escaped Cre-driven recombination during embryogenesis (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by photographs of mice shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Hair from Smarca4mel−/− mice shows an absence of melanin.
source: Examination of the hair from two genotypes showed an absence of melanin in Smarca4mel−/− hair.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy examination of hair.

claim: There is no staining with Dct and Sox10 antibodies in Smarca4mel−/− hair follicle bulbs.
source: We labelled the hair follicles of the Smarca4mel+/− or Smarca4mel−/− animals with antibodies against Dct and Sox10. In Smarca4mel+/− mice, Sox10 stained the nucleus of mature bulb melanocytes whose cytoplasm was stained with Dct (Figure 4C). In contrast, there was no staining with these antibodies in Smarca4mel−/− bulbs.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There are no identifiable mature melanocytes in Smarca4mel−/− animals.
source: There were therefore no identifiable mature melanocytes in the mutant animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of Dct and Sox10 staining in the hair follicles.

claim: BRG1 is essential for generation of mature melanocytes in vivo.
source: Taken together with the essential role of BRG1 in melanoma and melanocyte cells in vitro, these data indicate that BRG1 is essential for generation of mature melanocytes in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vivo mouse data showing absence of melanocytes in BRG1 knockout mice and the in vitro data showing BRG1 is essential for melanocyte and melanoma cell proliferation.

claim: More than 42,400 BRG1-occupied sites were identified in 501Mel cells.
source: We performed BRG1 ChIP-seq on native Mnase-digested chromatin along with a GFP-control ChIP-seq and identified >42,400 BRG1-occupied sites located in inter and intragenic regions, but with relative enrichment at the promoter (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: BRG1-occupied sites are located in inter and intragenic regions, but with relative enrichment at the promoter.
source: We performed BRG1 ChIP-seq on native Mnase-digested chromatin along with a GFP-control ChIP-seq and identified >42,400 BRG1-occupied sites located in inter and intragenic regions, but with relative enrichment at the promoter (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data and genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: BRG1-occupied sites often co-localize with or flank enhancer regions marked with H3K27ac.
source: Comparison with public ENCODE data showed BRG1-occupied sites often co-localized with or flanking enhancer regions marked with acetylated H3K27(ac) a mark of active enhancers (Smith and Shilatifard, 2014) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by integration of BRG1 ChIP-seq data with public ENCODE H3K27ac data.

claim: BRG1 co-localizes with around 15,000 melanocyte/melanoma H3K27ac marked regions at promoters as well as distal inter and intragenic enhancers.
source: The primary melanocyte and proliferative melanoma H3K27ac profiles are very similar and BRG1 co-localized with around 15,000 melanocyte/melanoma H3K27ac marked regions at promoters as well as distal inter and intragenic enhancers (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by integration of BRG1 ChIP-seq data with melanocyte and melanoma H3K27ac data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The most abundant transcription factor binding motifs at BRG1 peaks are NRF1, KLF5, SP1-family factors, CTCF, EGR1, and E-boxes.
source: Analysis of DNA sequence motifs at BRG1 peaks identified binding sites for a large set of transcription factors (TFs), the most abundant of which are NRF1, KLF5, SP1-family factors, CTCF, EGR1, and E-boxes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of BRG1 ChIP-seq peaks shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: BRG1 is recruited by many different transcription factors to its sites on the 501Mel genome.
source: Thus, BRG1 is recruited by many different TFs to its sites on the 501Mel genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of multiple different TF binding motifs at BRG1-occupied sites.

claim: BRG1 occupies sites as paired BRG1-bound nucleosomes separated by distances of 450–800 bp.
source: A set of highly occupied sites (Clusters A–C, Figure 5C) comprised two peaks separated by various distances. Re-clustering of each of these sets revealed a complex profile comprising in general two more or less sharply defined peaks separated by distances of 450–800 bp (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis of BRG1 ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: BRG1 is preferentially located at −200 bp and +72 bp relative to the TSS.
source: The metaprofile of all BRG1-occupied TSS showed preferential location of BRG1 at −200 bp and +72 bp relative to the TSS (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by meta-profile analysis of BRG1 occupancy at TSS shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The peak of promoter paused Pol II is located immediately upstream of the BRG1-bound +1 nucleosome.
source: Integration of RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) ChIP-seq data from 501Mel cells showed the peak of promoter paused Pol II located immediately upstream of the BRG1-bound +1 nucleosome.
evidence: This is supported by integration of BRG1 and Pol II ChIP-seq data.

claim: 34% of genes down-regulated upon BRG1 silencing have at least one BRG1-occupied site at ±10 kb from the TSS.
source: Integration with RNA-seq data showed that 34% of genes down-regulated upon BRG1 silencing had at least one BRG1-occupied site at ±10 kb, while this figure attained 47% using the ±30 kb window.
evidence: This is supported by integration of BRG1 ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: 47% of genes down-regulated upon BRG1 silencing have at least one BRG1-occupied site at ±30 kb from the TSS.
source: Integration with RNA-seq data showed that 34% of genes down-regulated upon BRG1 silencing had at least one BRG1-occupied site at ±10 kb, while this figure attained 47% using the ±30 kb window.
evidence: This is supported by integration of BRG1 ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Of more than 16,000 MITF occupied sites, 5867 are co-occupied by BRG1.
source: Integration of BRG1 and MITF ChIP-seq data showed that of >16,000 MITF occupied sites, 5867 were co-occupied by BRG1 and were located in both inter and intragenic regions, but enriched at promoters (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by integration of BRG1 and MITF ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MITF-BRG1 co-occupied sites are located in both inter and intragenic regions, but enriched at promoters.
source: Integration of BRG1 and MITF ChIP-seq data showed that of >16,000 MITF occupied sites, 5867 were co-occupied by BRG1 and were located in both inter and intragenic regions, but enriched at promoters (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by integration of BRG1 and MITF ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At co-occupied sites, MITF binds between two BRG1 peaks.
source: At co-occupied sites, MITF binds between two BRG1 peaks as observed at the TYR locus (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing the relative positions of MITF and BRG1 peaks, as illustrated at the TYR locus in Figure 6C.

claim: E and M-boxes for MITF are enriched at MITF-BRG1 co-occupied sites.
source: Co-occupied sites showed enrichment not only in E and M-boxes for MITF, but also in motifs for SOX10, CREB, and ETS1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), TFs that may cooperate with MITF and BRG1 to regulate associated target genes.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of MITF-BRG1 co-occupied sites shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Motifs for SOX10, CREB, and ETS1 are enriched at MITF-BRG1 co-occupied sites.
source: Co-occupied sites showed enrichment not only in E and M-boxes for MITF, but also in motifs for SOX10, CREB, and ETS1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), TFs that may cooperate with MITF and BRG1 to regulate associated target genes.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of MITF-BRG1 co-occupied sites shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There are 1065 TSS where BRG1 occupies the nucleosomes flanking the TSS and MITF binds the nucleosome-depleted region.
source: In addition, we also identified a set of 1065 TSS, where BRG1 occupies the nucleosomes flanking the TSS and MITF binds the NDR (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Almost 6000 SOX10-occupied sites were detected in 501Mel cells.
source: Almost 6000 SOX10-occupied sites were detected, but unlike MITF they were mainly located at distal regulatory elements with only around 80 sites at the proximal promoter. (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by SOX10 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SOX10-occupied sites are mainly located at distal regulatory elements with only around 80 sites at the proximal promoter.
source: Almost 6000 SOX10-occupied sites were detected, but unlike MITF they were mainly located at distal regulatory elements with only around 80 sites at the proximal promoter. (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by SOX10 ChIP-seq data and genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SOX10 recognition motifs are strongly enriched at SOX10 bound sites.
source: SOX10 recognition motifs were strongly enriched at SOX10 bound sites some of which were organised as degenerate palindromes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of SOX10 ChIP-seq peaks shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Recognition motifs for TCF/LEF, MITF, and TFAP2A are enriched at SOX10 bound sites.
source: Recognition motifs for TCF/LEF, MITF, and TFAP2A were also enriched at these sites.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of SOX10 ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: SOX10 and MITF co-occupy 3674 sites.
source: SOX10 and MITF co-occupied 3674 sites where MITF was located either 3′ or 5′ to SOX10 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: SOX10, MITF, BRG1, and H3K27ac are found at 1929 sites.
source: SOX10, MITF, BRG1, and H3K27ac were found at 1929 sites (Figure 7A, clusters A–D) while varying levels of SOX10, MITF and BRG1 were found at an additional ≈2000 sites (cluster E), whereas SOX10 and BRG1 co-occupied 1159 sites (cluster F) and 972 sites displayed essentially only SOX10 (cluster G).
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 1929 MAREs at active melanocyte/melanoma enhancer elements are associated with 1511 genes involved in pigmentation, cell motility and adhesion, actin cytoskeleton organisation, and signalling.
source: The above data define a specific organisation of MITF-associated regulatory elements (MAREs) where MITF alone or with SOX10 bind between two BRG1-bound nucleosomes. This analysis also defined 1929 MAREs at active melanocyte/melanoma enhancer elements associated with 1511 genes involved in pigmentation, cell motility and adhesion, actin cytoskeleton organisation, and signalling (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis and gene ontology analysis.

claim: There is a large overlap between BRG1 and YY1 genome occupancy.
source: We also found a large overlap between BRG1 and YY1 genome occupancy (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 2853 sites show co-localization of YY1 with MITF.
source: Despite the fact that YY1 ChIP-seq was performed in a distinct melanoma line (Li et al., 2012), we identified 2853 sites where YY1 co-localized with MITF and 3060 SOX10-YY1 co-occupied sites (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 3060 sites show co-localization of SOX10 and YY1.
source: Despite the fact that YY1 ChIP-seq was performed in a distinct melanoma line (Li et al., 2012), we identified 2853 sites where YY1 co-localized with MITF and 3060 SOX10-YY1 co-occupied sites (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 1070 sites show co-localization of YY1, MITF, SOX10, and BRG1.
source: All three proteins co-localize at 1070 sites together with BRG1 and 530 of these sites are marked with H3K27ac (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: 530 sites show co-localization of YY1, MITF, SOX10, BRG1, and H3K27ac.
source: All three proteins co-localize at 1070 sites together with BRG1 and 530 of these sites are marked with H3K27ac (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: TFAP2A is involved in melanoma.
source: TFAP2A is a TF involved in melanoma (Huang et al., 1998) and normal melanocyte function (Brewer et al., 2004; Van Otterloo et al., 2010) and co-localizes with MITF at promoters involved in pigment cell differentiation in primary human melanocytes (H Seberg, E van Otterloo, and RA Cornell, manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TFAP2A is involved in normal melanocyte function.
source: TFAP2A is a TF involved in melanoma (Huang et al., 1998) and normal melanocyte function (Brewer et al., 2004; Van Otterloo et al., 2010) and co-localizes with MITF at promoters involved in pigment cell differentiation in primary human melanocytes (H Seberg, E van Otterloo, and RA Cornell, manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TFAP2A co-localizes with MITF at promoters involved in pigment cell differentiation in primary human melanocytes.
source: TFAP2A is a TF involved in melanoma (Huang et al., 1998) and normal melanocyte function (Brewer et al., 2004; Van Otterloo et al., 2010) and co-localizes with MITF at promoters involved in pigment cell differentiation in primary human melanocytes (H Seberg, E van Otterloo, and RA Cornell, manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This is supported by citation to unpublished work.

claim: TFAP2A binding motifs are enriched at BRG1 bound sites.
source: In addition, TFAP2A binding motifs are enriched at BRG1 bound sites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Of 13,693 TFAP2A-bound sites in human melanocytes, 6432 sites co-localize with BRG1 and H3K27ac.
source: In agreement with this, of the 13,693 TFAP2A-bound sites in human melanocytes, 6432 sites co-localized with BRG1 and H3K27ac defining a large set of active TFAP2A-bound regulatory elements (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At more than 1000 sites, MITF is located at varying distances 5′ or 3′ to TFAP2A.
source: Also, at more than 1000 sites, MITF was located at varying distances 5′ or 3′ to TFAP2A, and YY1 and TFAP2A colocalized at 4819 sites (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: YY1 and TFAP2A colocalize at 4819 sites.
source: Also, at more than 1000 sites, MITF was located at varying distances 5′ or 3′ to TFAP2A, and YY1 and TFAP2A colocalized at 4819 sites (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: 762 YY1-TFAP2A sites are also occupied by BRG1 and MITF and marked by H3K27ac.
source: Integrative analysis identified 762 YY1-TFAP2A sites also occupied by BRG1 and MITF and marked by H3K27ac, defining a set of TFAP2A-YY1-containing MAREs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by integrative ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: siMITF silencing leads to specific loss of BRG1 at a promoter proximal site at the TYR locus.
source: At the TYR locus, siMITF silencing led to the specific loss of BRG1 at a promoter proximal site (* in Figure 8A), whereas at the upstream site where MITF co-localized with SOX10 little change was observed (arrowheads in Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by BRG1 ChIP-seq data following siMITF silencing shown in Figure 8A.

claim: siSOX10 silencing diminishes BRG1 at all sites at the TYR locus.
source: In contrast, siSOX10 and consequent loss of both SOX10 and MITF (see above), diminished BRG1 at all sites.
evidence: This is supported by BRG1 ChIP-seq data following siSOX10 silencing.

claim: BRG1 is recruited to SOX10/MITF sites and may spread across the locus.
source: Interestingly, BRG1 occupancy was observed throughout the region between these sites. siSOX10 silencing led to BRG1 loss across the entire region suggesting that it is recruited to the SOX10/MITF sites and then may spread across the locus.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of BRG1 loss upon siSOX10 silencing.

claim: MITF and SOX10 independently or cooperatively recruit BRG1 to a large number of genomic loci.
source: A global analysis identified sites showing a strong and preferential loss of BRG1 following, siSOX10 (clusters B and G–H, Figure 8C), siMITF (clusters E and F) or both, (cluster D), defining sites where MITF and SOX10 independently or cooperatively recruit BRG1 (Figure 8D). These data indicate that MITF and SOX10 actively recruit BRG1 either cooperatively or specifically to a large number of genomic loci.
evidence: This is supported by global analysis of BRG1 ChIP-seq data following siMITF or siSOX10 silencing shown in Figures 8C and 8D.

claim: BRG1 recruitment by MITF at SERPINE1 and IL24 loci acts to silence their expression.
source: Expression of SERPINE1 and IL24, two SASP components, was strongly up-regulated in senescent siMITF cells (see above). At both loci, BRG1 and MITF were present at either the promoter and/or distal regulatory regions and were lost upon siMITF coinciding with activation of their expression (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–B). These observations suggest that BRG1 recruitment by MITF at these genes acts to silence their expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of MITF and BRG1 at these loci coincides with gene activation.

claim: BRG1 is re-localized over the genome to new sites during siMITF-induced senescence.
source: Furthermore, BRG1 was re-localized over the genome to new sites during this process for example to CCL2 that was strongly induced upon siMITF silencing (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by BRG1 ChIP-seq data showing increased BRG1 occupancy at CCL2 in siMITF cells shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Nuclear receptor half sites are enriched at MITF-bound sites associated with both up and down regulated genes.
source: We also noted that different sequence motifs were enriched at MITF-bound sites associated with either up or down regulated genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D). In particular, we observed that nuclear receptor half sites were enriched at loci associated with both classes.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: BRG1 silencing results in increased MITF occupancy at many co-occupied sites.
source: Anti-HA ChIP-qPCR at MITF sites not associated with BRG1 co-occupancy showed only a mild reduction in MITF occupancy (Figure 9A, group A). In contrast, at many co-occupied sites, BRG1 silencing resulted in a marked increase in MITF occupancy.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: BRG1 regulates the dynamics of MITF binding to a subset of sites.
source: Thus, BRG1 regulates the dynamics of MITF binding to a subset of sites
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that BRG1 loss affects MITF occupancy at some but not all co-occupied sites.

claim: MITF associates with PBAF in the soluble nuclear fraction.
source: Moreover, we show that MITF associates with PBAF in the soluble nuclear fraction suggesting that they form a complex in the nucleoplasm and are recruited simultaneously to the chromatin to create the NDRs (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by the tandem affinity purification data showing MITF-PBAF interaction in the soluble nuclear extract.

claim: MITF and PBAF are recruited simultaneously to chromatin to create nucleosome-depleted regions.
source: Moreover, we show that MITF associates with PBAF in the soluble nuclear fraction suggesting that they form a complex in the nucleoplasm and are recruited simultaneously to the chromatin to create the NDRs (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MITF and PBAF interact in the soluble nuclear fraction before binding to chromatin.
